For a square pattern shifted by a constant, compare each term with its position squared.

A sequence like one fifth, two fifths, three fifths has nth term n divided by 5.

Squaring or cubing acts on the position number. To generate an unfamiliar term, substitute its position into the rule.

examples.title: Find the nth term of a linear sequence
examples.question:
Here are the first terms of a linear sequence: \(\frac{7}{2}\), \(6\), \(\frac{17}{2}\), \(11\).

  1. Give the value of term 5.

    [2]

  2. Write the nth term rule in n.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The common difference is \(\frac{5}{2}\).

The rule is \(\frac{5}{2}n+1\) because position 1 gives \(\frac{7}{2}\).

\(\frac{27}{2}\)

(b) Check that the rule changes by \(\frac{5}{2}\) per term.

\(\frac{5}{2}n+1\)

examples.title: Use a rule in the forward direction
examples.question:
A function squares its input and adds 2. Consider the input -5.

  1. Find the output.

    [2]

  2. Does the input 5 produce the same output? Explain.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) -5 squared is 25.

Add 2.

\(27\)

(b) It is possible for two inputs to have one shared output. Each input still has only one output.

examples.question:
A function takes a positive input, squares it and adds 3. The output is 52.

  1. Find the input.

    [2]

  2. Why is the negative square root not allowed here?

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) Subtract 3 to undo the addition. This gives 49.

Take the positive square root.

\(7\)

(b) When undoing a square, always check which inputs are allowed.

The inputs were restricted to positive numbers.

examples.title: Turn a rule into an equation

A tank has 5 litres at the start. Each filling cycle adds 9 litres. Let x be the number of cycles and y be the volume.

  1. Find y when x is 2.

  2. Give the equation in x and y.

examples.solution:

Add the initial 5 litres.

\(23\)

(b) The coefficient of x gives the change per cycle.

\(y=9x+5\)

examples.title: Find the equation of a drawn line
examples.question:
A straight line crosses the vertical axis at (0, 2) and passes through (5, 6).

  1. Find the gradient.

    [2]

  2. Write the equation of the line in y = mx + c form.

    [1]
examples.solution:

\(\frac{4}{5}\)

(b) The y-intercept is 2. Keep the sign and value of the gradient.

examples.title: Read a rate from a distance graph
examples.question:
A cycle route's distance–time graph is a straight line through the origin. After 10 minutes it reaches 60 metres.

  1. Find the speed in metres per minute.

    [2]

  2. Give the distance after one extra minute if this line continues.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) Calculate change in distance divided by elapsed time.

\(6\)

(b) One extra minute adds 6 metres.

66 metres.

examples.title: Compare two slopes
examples.question:
Two straight distance–time lines start at zero. Route A covers 20 m in 4 seconds. Route B covers 22 m in 4 seconds.

  1. By how many metres per second is route B faster?

    [2]

  2. Which line is steeper?

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) The speeds are \(5\) and \(\frac{11}{2}\) metres per second.

Compare the two speeds by subtraction.

\(\frac{1}{2}\)

(b) A bigger distance per second gives a larger gradient.

Route B.

examples.title: Read a mass-per-volume graph
examples.question:
A mass–volume graph through the origin includes the point with volume 5 cubic centimetres and mass 2 grams.

  1. Give the density in grams per cubic centimetre.

    [2]

  2. Describe a higher-density substance on the same axes.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) The gradient of a mass versus volume graph gives mass per unit volume.

\(\frac{2}{5}\)

(b) For a fixed volume, the more dense substance has a larger mass.

It has a steeper straight line through the origin.
